facts.raw_span: A 21-year-old woman with autism spectrum disorder (on risperidone) and intellectual disability
no prior history of syncope, cardiac arrest, or known cardiovascular disease
sinus rhythm with interpolated premature ventricular complexes and a QTc of 380 ms
ejection fraction of 45–50%, normal wall thickness, and no valvular abnormalities
A 21-year-old woman with autism spectrum disorder (on risperidone) and intellectual disability
no prior history of syncope, cardiac arrest, or known cardiovascular disease
sinus rhythm with interpolated premature ventricular complexes and a QTc of 380 ms
ejection fraction of 45–50%, normal wall thickness, and no valvular abnormalities

concepts.why: The patient's witnessed collapse and bystander ECG showing ventricular fibrillation, along with the electrocardiogram revealing a QTc of 380 ms, suggest Long QT Syndrome.

The patient's ejection fraction of 45-50% and normal wall thickness on echocardiography could be consistent with Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy, although the absence of valvular abnormalities and other specific features makes this diagnosis less likely.

The patient's witnessed collapse and bystander ECG showing ventricular fibrillation, along with the electrocardiogram revealing interpolated premature ventricular complexes, suggest Catecholaminergic Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia.
The patient's ejection fraction of 45-50% on echocardiography is consistent with Dilated Cardiomyopathy, although the absence of other specific features makes this diagnosis less likely.

rationales.F04: Ventricular fibrillation is a key feature of several cardiac conditions, including Long QT Syndrome and Catecholaminergic Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia.
rationales.F11: A QTc of 380 ms is prolonged, which is a key feature of Long QT Syndrome.
rationales.F12: An ejection fraction of 45-50% is reduced, which is consistent with Dilated Cardiomyopathy, but the normal wall thickness argues against Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy.
